Reading · friendship and communication

1.1 Discuss. How many of your online contacts have you actually met? Can an online friendship be as real as a face-to-face one?

Key words

a bond a strong feeling that connects people

superficial not deep or serious

vulnerable open about your weaknesses

an acquaintance someone you know a little

But Are They Real Friends?

The average social media user has several hundred “friends”. The average person, according to most research, has between three and five people they would call genuinely close. That gap says something important about the way we now talk to one another.

Critics of online friendship argue that it is superficial. You can follow someone for years, they say, and know their opinions, their holidays and their breakfast, while knowing almost nothing about their fears or their disappointments. Real closeness, this argument goes, is built in person — through silence as much as conversation, through being physically present when something goes wrong.

Yet the evidence is more complicated. Studies of long-distance friendships have found that people who communicate regularly online often report deeper conversations than those who meet occasionally in person, precisely because they are not distracted by circumstances. Anyone who has moved abroad knows the strange truth that a message at the right moment can matter more than a visit at the wrong one.

There is also the question of who benefits. For people who find face-to-face contact difficult — the shy, the ill, those living far from anyone who shares their interests — online friendship is not a poor substitute for the real thing. It is the real thing, and often the only version available. A teenager in a small town who finds three people online who understand her has not lost anything; she has found something.

Perhaps the honest conclusion is that the medium matters far less than the behaviour. A friendship in which both people are willing to be vulnerable will survive on almost any channel; one in which neither is will remain an acquaintance, however many coffees are shared. The question is not whether your friends are online. It is whether either of you has said anything that mattered this month.

Grammar · subject and object questions

Presentation

Compare two questions about the same sentence — Aziz called Malika.

SUBJECT question — we don't know the doer:

Who called Malika? → Aziz did. no do/does/did · word order like a statement

OBJECT question — we don't know the receiver:

Who did Aziz call? → Malika. auxiliary do/does/did + base verb

Subject question

Object question

What happened?

What did you do?

Who lives here?

Who do you live with?

Which team won?

Which team did you support?

How many people came?

How many people did you invite?

Error warning

Never add do/did to a subject question:

Who did write this message? ✗ Who wrote this message? ✓

Never leave it out of an object question:

Who you called? ✗ Who did you call? ✓

With be there is no auxiliary either way: Who is that? · Who were you with?

Gradable adjectives take very / quite / a bit: very good · quite tired · a bit cold.

Extreme adjectives already mean very, so they take absolutely / really:

absolutely brilliant · absolutely exhausted · really enormous

NOT very brilliant · NOT absolutely good

4

Everyday English · giving and responding to opinions

4.1 Read the conversation.

Sardor So what did you think of the new café?

Malika To be honest, I wasn't impressed. The coffee was cold.

Sardor Really? I thought it was great.

Malika Well, the cake was good, I'll give you that.

Sardor Exactly! And the atmosphere is lovely, don't you think?

Malika Hmm, I'm not so sure. It was very noisy.

Malika That's a fair point, though. I'd give it another try.

Giving an opinion

Agreeing

Disagreeing politely

To be honest, …

Exactly!

Really? I thought…

I thought (it was)…

Me too. / Me neither.

I'm not so sure.

If you ask me, …

That's a fair point.

I see what you mean, but…

Error warning

Me too after a positive statement · me neither after a negative one:

“I loved it.” — “Me too.” “I didn't like it.” — “Me neither.”
